title: CI/CD Pipelines
subtitle: Follow one small commit through build, test, artifact and deploy stages, then watch a bad release get rolled back.
learn: What each pipeline stage (build, test, artifact, deploy) is for and why the order matters
Why trunk-based development pairs with small, frequent merges
Why you build one artifact once and promote that same artifact to every environment
How pipeline-as-code makes delivery reviewable and repeatable
How rollback works and why it should be the fastest thing your pipeline does

steps.title: How does code reach users?
steps.body: A developer has just finished a 40-line change. How does it reach real users? Old-style teams saved up changes for weeks, handed a big release to an ops team, and hoped. A CI/CD pipeline replaces hope with a fixed, automated path from commit to production. CI (continuous integration) means merging small changes often and automatically checking every merge. CD (continuous delivery) means every change that passes is ready to ship.
steps.idea: A pipeline turns 'ship it' from a risky event into a boring, repeatable routine.
steps.caption: One small change is ready to leave the developer's laptop.

steps.title: Merge small, merge often
steps.body: Trunk-based development means everyone merges into one shared main branch (the trunk) at least once a day. Branches live for hours, not weeks, so they rarely drift apart and merge conflicts stay tiny. Half-finished work hides behind a feature flag (an on/off switch in the code) instead of a long-lived branch. In the animation the developer pushes to main, and the repo sends a webhook to CI: an automatic HTTP call that says 'something changed, start the pipeline'. Many teams also run a quick set of checks on the pull request first.
steps.idea: Small changes are easier to review, to test and to undo, so trunk-based development makes everything downstream cheaper.
steps.caption: The push lands on main, and a webhook wakes the CI runner.

steps.title: Build in a clean runner
steps.body: The CI runner is a build machine. It starts fresh, checks out the exact commit, restores cached dependencies, compiles the code and packages it as a candidate container image tagged with the commit SHA (the commit's unique hash): shop-api:a1b2c3d. A clean machine exposes 'works on my laptop' bugs. A linter (a tool that spots style slips and obvious mistakes) fails in seconds, so a typo never waits behind a long test suite. In this example, with caching, the build takes about 2 minutes.
steps.idea: Build in a clean, pinned environment (exact dependency and tool versions, not 'latest') so the result depends only on the commit.
steps.caption: A clean runner builds commit a1b2c3d into an image in about 2 min.

steps.title: Run the gates
steps.body: Now the pipeline tests that exact candidate image. Quick checks go first: lint, unit tests, and fast security and dependency scans. Slower integration tests follow. If anything fails, the pipeline stops and nothing ships. A red (failing) main branch means stop the line: fix or revert right away. Say 1,240 tests pass in about 6 minutes on parallel runners (many machines sharing the work), so the pipeline clock reads 8 minutes. Keep this stage under roughly 10 minutes. The testing lesson covers test design.
steps.idea: Order stages cheapest-first and fail fast, so feedback arrives in minutes.
steps.caption: All 1,240 tests pass on parallel runners; the clock reads 8 min.

steps.title: Publish the tested artifact
steps.body: CI pushes the image that passed the gates to the artifact registry, a store for built images. It is the very same image, so nothing is rebuilt after testing. A tag can be moved to point at another image, so deployments should reference the content digest (a hash of the image) or the registry should enforce immutable tags. Every environment runs this one image; settings and secrets are added at deploy time, not baked in. Rebuilding could pull different dependencies than the ones you tested. Pushing and verifying adds about 2 minutes, so the clock reads 10.
steps.idea: Build once, test that artifact, then promote it everywhere; only injected configuration differs between environments.
steps.caption: Image shop-api:a1b2c3d is stored in the registry; the clock reads 10 min.

steps.title: Staging, then production
steps.body: The pipeline first deploys the image to staging, a rehearsal copy of production, and runs smoke tests: log in, load a page, place a test order. If they pass, the same image is promoted to production, automatically (continuous deployment) or after a human approves (continuous delivery). The pipeline is itself a YAML file in the repo (pipeline as code), so changes get pull request review, can be diffed and reverted, and secrets are injected at run time, never committed. Canary rollouts are in the deploys lesson. Staging, smoke tests and the production rollout add about 4 minutes: about 14 in total.
steps.idea: Pipeline as code makes the delivery process reviewable, versioned and identical on every run.
steps.caption: The same image runs in staging, then in production.

steps.title: The release is bad
steps.body: Suppose the change passed every test but has a bug that only real traffic exposes. On the diagram, production turns red: the error rate climbs from 0.2% to 6%. Tests cannot catch everything, which is why watching production is part of the pipeline's feedback loop. A fix-forward patch (a new fix instead of undoing the release) needs time to write and review, then another full pipeline run of about 14 minutes, while customers keep failing. Observability is its own lesson; here the point is that something must trigger the next move.
steps.idea: Passing tests means 'probably fine'; production signals decide whether it really is.
steps.caption: Errors in production jump from 0.2% to 6%.

steps.title: Redeploy the last good image
steps.body: The registry still holds the previous image, so a rollback is just a deploy of shop-api:9f8e7d6, with no rebuild and no new tests. In the animation production pulls that old image, and the error rate drops back to 0.2% in about a minute. Roll back configuration changes too, and watch health checks and the error rate after the redeploy. This works only if old images are kept and the release did not change data in a way the old code cannot read. A one-way database change makes rollback unsafe, which is why expand/contract migrations exist. Roll back first, then debug calmly.
steps.idea: Rollback should be a one-step redeploy of a stored artifact, usually much faster than fixing forward.
steps.caption: Production pulls the previous image and is healthy again; errors back to 0.2%.

steps.title: The path from commit to users
steps.body: Merge small changes to trunk often. The pipeline builds one candidate in a clean runner, tests it cheapest-first, publishes that same image, and promotes it through staging to production. The pipeline itself is code in the repo. When production signals go bad, redeploy the previous image first and investigate second.
steps.idea: Small changes, one artifact, automated gates, and a fast way back.
steps.caption: Commit to production in about 14 minutes, with a rollback in about 1.

quiz.q: Staging passed all smoke tests, but the pipeline then rebuilds the code from source for production. What is the main risk?
options: Production will be slower to start
The production build may differ from what was tested, for example through newer dependency versions
Staging data will leak into production
The registry will run out of space
quiz.why: Rebuilding creates a new artifact that was never tested. Building once and promoting the same image guarantees production runs exactly what staging validated.

quiz.q: Your pipeline runs a 25-minute end-to-end suite before the 30-second lint check. What is the best change?
options: Remove the lint check
Run the end-to-end suite only after deploying to production
Skip tests on small changes
Run lint and unit tests first to fail fast, and parallelise or trim the slow suite
quiz.why: Cheapest-first ordering gives quick failure feedback. Keep slow suites in the pipeline, but shard them in parallel or trim them, instead of removing the per-change gate.

quiz.q: A team keeps feature branches open for three weeks, then merges. Which problem does trunk-based development mainly address?
options: Slow network speed to the registry
Missing database indexes
Large, conflict-prone merges and big risky releases
Too many environments
quiz.why: Long-lived branches diverge, causing painful merges and large untested batches. Merging small changes daily keeps integration cheap and each release small.

quiz.q: A release raises production errors to 6%. The previous image is still in the registry. What is usually the best first move?
options: Write and ship a fix through the full pipeline
Redeploy the previous artifact, then investigate
Delete the failing tests
Rebuild the old commit from source
quiz.why: Redeploying a stored, known-good artifact restores service in about a minute. Fix-forward takes a full pipeline run while users keep failing.

quiz.q: When might rolling back the application image NOT be enough to undo a release?
options: When the image was tagged with a commit SHA
When staging is down
When tests ran in parallel
When the release also ran a one-way database migration that the old code cannot work with
quiz.why: Code rolls back easily, but data changes do not. Backward-compatible, expand/contract migrations keep the old version working against the new schema.

cheatsheet.def: Merge to a shared main branch often, and automatically build and test every merge.
Delivery: every passing change is ready to ship, release is a button. Deployment: it ships to production automatically.
Everyone merges to main at least daily; unfinished work hides behind feature flags, not long branches.
A versioned build output (image, package) tagged by commit SHA, built once and promoted unchanged through environments.
The pipeline definition (YAML) lives in the repo, so it is reviewed, versioned and reproducible.
Order stages cheapest-first (lint, unit, integration, e2e) so most failures show up within minutes.
Redeploy the previous known-good artifact. Needs retained artifacts and backward-compatible data changes.
Aim for commit to test result in under 10 minutes and a rollback in a few minutes at most; these are guidelines, not standards.
